text:
Image-only reading of packet 06

Orientation and surviving material
All six images were viewed. Image-001 is an upright binding overview; images 002–004 enlarge successive parts of the exposed strip at its right edge. The writing and music in that strip are upright and read left to right. Purple-and-gold covering material conceals almost the entire width of the manuscript. Images 005 and 006 show the upper and lower left corners of the same covering: 005 has two exposed red line segments but no readable notes or words; 006 has no readable music or words.

The exposed music uses black angular noteheads and stems on red five-line staves. Five lines can be counted particularly clearly in image-004. Approximately seven staff-level bands survive in the right strip in image-001, including the band beside the large red initial. The left ends of the musical systems are hidden. I cannot securely identify a clef or its line. The tall black marks with a broad head and descending stem in the clear runs appear to be notes, not securely identifiable clefs. No absolute pitch is assigned.

Passage 1: strongest continuous run
Image-004, upper quarter, approximately x=160–345, y=175–305; also visible near the bottom of the strip in image-001.
Four consecutive noteheads: 0, -1, -2, -3.
These are successive diatonic staff positions relative to the first head, with upward pitch positive. Adjacent changes: -1, -1, -1. The first head lies in the space between the top two red staff lines; the next is on the second line from the top, the third in the following space, and the fourth on the middle line. The first head has a long descending stem. That stem is not an additional note. The subsequent three heads are distinct, descending angular/diamond forms. I see no intervening repeated noteheads. This is a reasonably secure four-note descending run, and it remains four notes after repeated pitches collapse. It begins immediately beside the covering, so preceding music is hidden. I stop at the fourth note; no continuation is exposed.
The last diamond is grouped closely with the descending notes and does not have an obvious separate custos form; nevertheless, because this is the end of an exposed system, a terminal guide-note interpretation cannot be excluded from shape alone.
Literal text: above this staff is an ending resembling "…tur" (last letters not wholly secure). Below it only a damaged final character resembling "a" is exposed. I do not join these into a completed word.

Passage 2: shorter descending group
Image-002, lower-middle portion, approximately x=215–345, y=990–1115; the staff directly above the large red initial.
Three exposed noteheads: 0, -1, -2.
Adjacent changes: -1, -1. The first is a broad head with a long descending stem; the two following diamond-shaped heads descend by successive staff steps. Local line curvature and the sloping first head make exact centering less clean than in passage 1, but the consecutive descending contour is clear. There is no fourth exposed head in this group. Do not count the first note's stem as another note.
Literal text beneath: "…atur" (the beginning is hidden). The large red initial below resembles "A"; this is a visible letter, not an identification of the text. Above this musical group, the earlier line's ending resembles "…ma".

Other exposed marks and why they are not long readings
Image-002, upper musical band around y=360–650: one large stemmed note is exposed near x=250; a small isolated dark mark much farther right, on the curved edge near y=450, might be a custos. Its form and staff alignment are too uncertain for a dependable sequence, and the intervening covered part must not be supplied.

Image-003, upper staff around y=260–540: a partial black mark touches the covering at the left, and an isolated small angular mark is farther right near y=525. The latter could be a custos. The visible parts do not establish a reliable consecutive melody. Beneath them I can read only an uncertain ending, approximately "…lia" or "…tia".

Image-003, middle staff around y=705–950: there is a clipped compound shape near the covering followed by a stemmed head farther right. A possible local reading is 0, -1, 0, if the two lobes of the clipped shape represent separate heads; this is LOW confidence and should not be treated as an independent secure three-note passage. The left edge of the first form is hidden, and the internal head division is uncertain. The text below resembles "…am", but the leftmost letter is clipped.

Image-003, lower staff around y=1130–1380: one clear stemmed head is exposed near x=205, with a small isolated mark close to the right vertical ruling near x=345. That smaller mark might be a custos rather than a sung note. It appears approximately one staff step below the first head (tentative 0, -1), but I would not use this as a continuous melodic run. A tall narrow stroke at the right is not safely countable as a note. Beneath is the ending resembling "…tur", also repeated at the top of image-004 because the crops overlap.

The band beside the large red initial is heavily curved and worn; its dark strokes are insufficient to distinguish notes from other marks. No melody is supplied for it.

Coverage and limitations
Viewed images 001, 002, 003, 004, 005, and 006 individually. These are overlapping views of one mostly covered manuscript strip, not six independent passages. One usable four-note relative-pitch run survives, plus a clear three-note descending group. Nothing exposed supports a continuous six-to-fourteen-note transcription. The obstruction, rather than general image failure, limits length. Clefs, beginnings of words, and most music are hidden. I have not bridged covered spans, supplied any text from memory, or inferred an identity.
